title: Seventy-minute introductory lecture
instruction: Create a 70-minute introductory lecture outline on variables and assignment for freshman programming students. Include a sequence with realistic time allocations.

expected_characteristics.description: States measurable objectives.
Uses a worked example before guided and independent practice.
Allocates time that totals approximately 70 minutes.
Ends with synthesis.

title: Continue from prior material
instruction: Plan the opening and progression for a lecture introducing functions. Explicitly connect the lesson to the previous class and avoid reteaching all prior material.
context: Previous class: variables, assignment statements, and tracing a short sequential program. Students have not yet defined their own functions.

expected_characteristics.description: Retrieves variables or assignment as a bridge to parameters and return values.
Distinguishes known prerequisites from new function concepts.
Provides a coherent progression into function definitions.

title: Lecture built around objectives
instruction: Create a lesson sequence for these objectives: identify a Boolean expression, evaluate one using a truth table, and use a condition in a simple if statement. Show where each objective is taught and checked.

expected_characteristics.description: All three objectives visibly map to instruction and a check for understanding.
Moves from expression meaning to truth tables and then code.
Includes at least one worked example and learner practice.

title: Avoid excessive abstraction
instruction: Teach freshmen the idea of algorithmic efficiency using a short introductory lecture. Do not assume discrete mathematics, logarithms, or prior formal analysis. Introduce only the abstraction needed to compare simple approaches.

expected_characteristics.description: Begins with a concrete comparison such as checking items one by one.
Avoids unnecessary advanced notation and unexplained prerequisites.
Builds toward a modest generalization in supported steps.

title: Slides from supplied networking material
instruction: Turn the supplied material into a logical slide progression for freshmen. Separate slide text from optional speaker notes.
source_material: A domain name is a human-readable name for an internet resource. DNS translates a domain name into an IP address that computers use to route network traffic. A DNS resolver asks DNS servers for the matching record. A cached answer may be reused until its time-to-live expires.

expected_characteristics.description: Connects domain names, DNS lookup, IP addresses, and resolution in a sensible order.
Uses concise slide text with details in notes where appropriate.
Does not introduce unsupported networking protocols.

title: Concise slides from dense source
instruction: Create at most six slides from the material. Keep each slide to a title and no more than three short bullets; place explanation in speaker notes rather than adding more bullets.
source_material: A variable is a named reference to a value used by a program. Assignment evaluates an expression and stores or binds its resulting value to a name. In Python, the equals sign is assignment rather than a mathematical claim of equality. A later assignment can rebind a name. Expressions can use values and names, and their evaluation follows operator precedence. A variable's value can be traced by following assignments in order. Descriptive names can make code easier to read. Variables do not necessarily represent fixed memory locations across all programming languages.

expected_characteristics.description: Uses at most six slides and at most three short bullets per slide.
Preserves the distinction between assignment and mathematical equality.
Places elaboration in notes rather than overcrowding slide text.

title: Slide outline with worked example
instruction: Create a concise slide outline introducing binary search to students who already understand sorted lists and linear search. Include one worked trace and a short practice opportunity.

expected_characteristics.description: States that binary search requires sorted data.
Traces a concrete search while showing how the search interval changes.
Uses concise slides and includes learner practice.

title: Slide sequence with conceptual progression
instruction: Outline slides for teaching a beginner how a database table, row, column, and a simple SELECT query relate. Order the ideas so each slide prepares for the next.

expected_characteristics.description: Establishes table structure before introducing query syntax.
Uses one major idea per slide and keeps wording clear.
Includes a simple example query tied to the introduced table.

title: Explain recursion to freshmen
instruction: Explain recursion to freshmen who know functions but have not seen recursive calls. Start with a concrete example, then name the general idea. Avoid assuming trees or mathematical induction.

expected_characteristics.description: Explains a base case and a smaller recursive step accurately.
Uses a small worked trace before generalizing.
Does not rely on unintroduced trees or induction.

title: Re-explain after confusion
instruction: A student says, 'I still don't understand why changing the list inside a function changed it outside.' Explain this again without repeating the same wording. Use a tiny example and check understanding.
context: The class has learned variables, function parameters, and basic Python lists. Mutable objects have not been formally named yet.

expected_characteristics.description: Acknowledges the confusion and changes explanatory approach.
Uses an accurate, appropriately scoped example of list mutation and function arguments.
Avoids unsupported memory-address jargon and checks understanding.

title: Correct a networking misconception
instruction: Respond to a student who says, 'DNS is the same thing as the internet because it finds websites.' Correct the misconception respectfully and explain DNS's role with a concrete analogy and a quick check question.

expected_characteristics.description: Distinguishes DNS name resolution from internet connectivity and web content.
Corrects without shaming and uses a fitting example.
Includes a check that reveals whether the distinction is understood.

title: Connect new concept to prior learning
instruction: Explain how a Python function's return value relates to expressions and assignment, concepts students learned last week. Make the connection explicit before introducing a new example.
context: Students can evaluate simple expressions and assign values to variables. They have just begun writing functions.

expected_characteristics.description: Explicitly connects returned values to expression evaluation and assignment.
Distinguishes printing output from returning a value.
Uses a small coherent example.

title: Guided lab following a lecture
instruction: Create a 60-minute guided lab that follows an introductory lecture on Python lists. Include checkpoints, expected observations, and a final independent extension.
context: Students have practiced variables, indexing, and simple loops. This is their first lab focused on lists.

expected_characteristics.description: Sequences supported tasks before independent application.
Includes checkpoints that reveal common indexing or mutation mistakes.
Activities fit the requested duration and connect to lecture content.

title: Build on a previous lab
instruction: Design the next 50-minute lab after students have created a basic contact list program. Extend their existing work rather than restarting from a blank file. Add one new requirement at a time.
context: Previous lab: students wrote a menu-driven program that stores names in a list and can add or display names. They have not used dictionaries.

expected_characteristics.description: Starts from and extends the existing program.
Introduces no more than one major new concept at once.
Avoids requiring dictionaries without instruction or scaffolding.

title: Lab requiring application
instruction: Create a beginner lab on conditional logic where students must apply the idea to make decisions, not merely copy a sequence of code. Include a small worked setup, then progressively less guidance.

expected_characteristics.description: Tasks require students to choose and justify conditions.
Support decreases gradually from worked example to independent task.
Avoids giving the full solution for every task.

title: Cross-concept classroom activity
instruction: Design a 60-minute active classroom activity connecting variables, conditionals, and loops. Include a clear progression from recall to application and finish with a synthesis discussion.
context: All three concepts have been taught in prior classes; students have traced short programs but have limited independent coding experience.

expected_characteristics.description: Includes a progression and plausible timing that totals about 60 minutes.
Requires learners to retrieve and combine all three concepts.
Ends with synthesis rather than an abrupt stop.

title: Activity with staged progression
instruction: Create a 55-minute small-group activity for learning how a simple web request moves from a browser to a server and back. Include checkpoints and a final synthesis in which groups explain the complete sequence.

expected_characteristics.description: Builds the sequence in stages before asking groups to explain the whole exchange.
Includes active participation and checks for understanding.
Keeps protocol details at an introductory level.

title: Explain exercise answers
instruction: Write an instructor guide for reviewing a short exercise that asks students to trace a loop and predict its output. Explain the reasoning for each step, not just the final output, and suggest questions to ask the class.
source_material: Exercise: total = 0; for value in [2, 3, 4]: total = total + value; print(total)

expected_characteristics.description: Traces each iteration accurately and reaches 9.
Makes the changing values visible for instruction.
Uses questions that reveal student reasoning.

title: Misconceptions and alternate examples
instruction: Prepare an instructor guide for teaching database primary keys. List likely beginner misconceptions and provide alternate examples to clarify the concept if the first explanation does not work.

expected_characteristics.description: Explains uniqueness and identification without claiming every key must be meaningful to users.
Identifies realistic misconceptions and pairs them with helpful alternate examples.
Keeps the guide suitable for introductory learners.

title: Formative questions for SQL
instruction: Create five short formative questions for an introductory lesson on SELECT, FROM, and WHERE. Include a concise expected answer and identify what misunderstanding each question can reveal.

expected_characteristics.description: Questions assess the supplied SQL concepts at an introductory level.
Includes answers and interpretable misconception signals.
Varies question form rather than repeating one pattern.

title: Homework restricted to taught material
instruction: Create a short homework assignment using only the supplied material. Do not require outside concepts or tools. State the relevant source section for each task and include an instructor-only answer key.
source_material: A database table contains rows and columns. SELECT names columns to return. FROM names a table. WHERE filters rows using a condition. Example: SELECT name FROM students WHERE active = 1;

expected_characteristics.description: Every task can be completed from the supplied material alone.
Does not introduce joins, aggregation, or unprovided SQL syntax.
Separates student-facing tasks from the answer key.

title: Freshman-level practice set
instruction: Write four short exercises on variables and assignment for freshmen. Move from basic tracing to one modest application. Avoid nested data structures and advanced syntax.

expected_characteristics.description: Exercises progress in difficulty without a sudden conceptual jump.
Uses only introductory variables and assignment.
Instructions are clear and answers are objectively checkable.

title: Identify prerequisites for complexity
instruction: Before planning an introductory lesson on algorithmic efficiency, identify the knowledge students need, distinguish essential from optional prerequisites, and propose a quick check for each essential prerequisite.
context: Students can trace loops and compare counts but have not studied logarithms or formal proofs.

expected_characteristics.description: Prioritizes tracing and basic counting rather than treating advanced math as essential.
Separates essential prerequisites from useful enrichment.
Proposes checks aligned to each stated prerequisite.

title: Notice a missing prerequisite
instruction: Review this proposed exercise and identify any knowledge it assumes that may not have been taught. Explain what should be introduced or scaffolded before students attempt it.
context: Taught so far: variables, if/else, and for loops. Not taught: lists, indexing, or functions.
source_material: Exercise proposal: Write a function that receives a list of temperatures, uses a list comprehension to keep values above a threshold, and returns the filtered list.

expected_characteristics.description: Flags functions, lists, indexing or iteration over collections, and list comprehensions as untaught or assumed concepts.
Suggests a plausible teaching or scaffolding sequence.
Does not assume the proposed exercise is appropriate as-is.

title: Explain using only supplied material
instruction: Use only the supplied material to explain how DNS resolution works. If the source does not answer a question, say what is not specified rather than filling the gap from outside knowledge.
source_material: A domain name is a human-readable name for an internet resource. DNS translates a domain name into an IP address. A resolver asks DNS servers for a matching record. Cached answers may be reused until their time-to-live expires.

expected_characteristics.description: Uses only facts present in the source and does not invent details about record types or protocol exchanges.
Clearly marks unspecified details as not provided.
Explains the available facts clearly to a beginner.

title: Sequence from prior course material
instruction: Create the opening 20 minutes of a lesson on functions that explicitly builds from prior work on variables and assignment. Include one retrieval question and explain how it prepares learners for the new concept.
context: Prior lesson covered variable names, assignment, and evaluating expressions. Students have not yet written a function definition.

expected_characteristics.description: Uses a retrieval prompt about variables or expressions and makes its connection explicit.
Introduces functions after the known material is activated.
Does not assume students already know parameters or return values.
